newsitem.title: CHINA: Cambodia's king says abdication offer rejected.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's king says abdication offer rejected.

text.p: Cambodian King Norodom Sihanouk said on Wednesday that Second Prime Minister Hun Sen had rejected his offer to abdicate and he had called on the strongman ruler to bring peace to the impoverished country.

Sihanouk's call for peace came as Cambodian forces loyal to Hun Sen, who seized power last month in a coup, tightened a noose around the last bastion of royalist support as they closed in on a town near the border with Thailand.
Sihanouk's statements followed a meeting on Tuesday with a high-level Cambodian delegation led by Hun Sen at the monarch's palatial residence in Beijing, where he is receiving medical treatment.

"This delegation -- in particular his excellency Hun Sen -- assured N. Sihanouk of its fidelity and its support for the king, whose offer to abdicate it did not accept," Sihanouk said in a statement sent to reporters in Beijing.

Political analysts said Sihanouk's offer on Monday to abdicate could signal he did not want any part of Cambodia's political turmoil, sparked last month when Hun Sen overthrew the king's son and co-premier, Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
Analysts in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh also said that Hun Sen had long feared the widely revered king would give up the throne, enter politics and challenge him for power.

The king said Hun Sen's delegation, which included new First Prime Minister Ung Huot and acting head of state Chea Sim, had welcomed his decision to return to Cambodia soon to hold a Buddhist ceremony for peace and reconciliation.
"My departure for Cambodia will take place well before the end of August," Sihanouk said in an earlier statement.
Hun Sen met Sihanouk on Tuesday in what analysts said was a bid to try to secure the king's political blessing for his new government.
Hun Sen had previously ruled with Ranariddh in an uneasy coalition government that took power after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.
Sihanouk has so far withheld his stamp of approval for Hun Sen's administration, deriding newly appointed co-premier Ung Huot as a "puppet" and likening the situation in Cambodia to a "comedy".
In an earlier statement, Sihanouk said he had asked Hun Sen to end the violence in Cambodia and work toward national reconciliation.
"I asked all of them to try to make an effort to achieve peace, cool down the situation and end war, insecurity and violence," Sihanouk said.

The king said he had asked Hun Sen and Ung Huot "to somehow achieve non-violence, national reconciliation, peaceful co-existence, solidarity, mutual respect, respect for human rights and our national constitution".

In Phnom Penh, meanwhile, defence ministry spokesman Colonel Chum Sambath said government forces were getting closer to seizing the border town of O'Smach, the last major redoubt of troops loyal to the ousted prince.
Since overthrowing Ranariddh on July 6, Hun Sen has fought the prince for diplomatic approval overseas while pushing the remnants of his army to remote pockets of the country.

Ranariddh left the country shortly after the start of Hun Sen's grab for power, and many royalists fled to Thailand after the coup and subsequent crackdown in which some 40 of the prince's supporters were killed.
A Cambodian military court has since issued a warrant for Prince Ranariddh's arrest on charges of weapons smuggling.

Also on Wednesday, Chinese Premier Li Peng met Hun Sen and Chea Sim in the seaside resort of Beidaihe and urged the Cambodian leaders to respect the king and work for a peaceful resolution to the country's problems.
Hun Sen is scheduled to return to Phnom Penh on Thursday.
